chunks: "A ground plane does a lot more than serve as zero volts. First, it's the return path.
At high frequency the return current flows right under each signal, which keeps loops small and so reduces radiation, pickup and crosstalk.
Second, it gives traces a defined characteristic impedance, since microstrip and stripline need a reference plane.
Third, it shields: a plane between two signal layers keeps their fields from coupling, and it terminates the electric field of traces above it.
Fourth, next to a power plane it forms a capacitor that helps high-frequency decoupling.
Fifth, it's a heat spreader, because copper conducts heat much better than FR-4; a plane under a hot chip with thermal vias is the standard way to cool it.
Sixth, it's a low-inductance path for ESD and surge current, so a strike at a connector can be shunted to ground without blowing up a chip.
Seventh, it balances the copper on the board so it doesn't warp. And for an antenna it's often the counterpoise, the other half of the radiator.
So when I'm tempted to cut a plane for routing, I think about which of those jobs I'm giving up."
